title: Strong earthquake shaking did not make baseflow recession faster at United States stream gauges (PGV of 10 cm/s or more, 1960-2026); a first-year low-flow increase is not confirmed
abstract: Question: After strong earthquake shaking, does baseflow recession become faster, and do low flows change, in the following months and years? Faster recession would show that shaking increased the drainage efficiency (permeability) of catchments. Approach: We used 367 ComCat earthquakes (M 5 or more, conterminous United States, 1960 to 2026), merged into 155 episodes, with USGS ShakeMap peak ground velocity (PGV) at USGS stream gauges and NWIS daily discharge for 5 years before and after each episode. Treated gauges had PGV of 10 cm/s or more. Control gauges had PGV below 1 cm/s within 200 km. We compared each event-year with the 5 baseline years (difference in differences). The plan was written before discharge data was downloaded. Findings: In the first year, the annual recession residual changed by -0.08 ln units (95 percent episode-bootstrap interval -0.15 to +0.06; 22 episodes, 105 treated gauges; Holm p 0.28). A within-episode year-permutation test gave p 0.11, and equal episode weights gave 0.00. Thus recession did not become faster. Recession on days 2 to 90 was slower (-0.22, -0.34 to -0.04; permutation p 0.11, or 0.005 with equal weights). The 7-day low flow rose by +0.33 ln (0.00 to +0.52; Holm p 0.10; permutation p 0.046), which failed the planned test. It was +0.20 without the 2001 Nisqually episode and +0.17 without the interference rule. Years 2 to 4 showed no clear change. False events before the earthquakes showed that the bootstrap intervals are too narrow. The result agrees with Manga (2001): shaking adds water without a lasting change in drainage efficiency, but the added-water signs are not confirmed. Limitations: about 100 treated gauges in 16 to 32 episodes; one episode supplies 39 percent of treated gauges; no rain data; model-based PGV for old events; many regulated gauges; reference-gauge subset of 4 to 7 episodes.
